paras: The lynching of Charles Stewart was the hanging of a Black man accused of murdering his wife, whom a mob took from the county jail at Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, about midnight on Monday, August 15, 1881. The local paper reported that the crowd demanding his death was made up of Black men and women, and a widely reprinted wire item said his father-in-law prayed for him and then helped hang him. The nearest newspaper condemned the lynching because Stewart had been awaiting trial in circuit court on circumstantial evidence.

Stewart had been jailed at Bay St. Louis on suspicion of killing his wife. On Monday he was brought before Justice Sylvester, who held him under a bond of $1,000 to appear at the circuit court, and when he could not give bond he was recommitted to jail. According to the Pascagoula Democrat-Star's correspondent, witnesses at the hearing described him as a man of "intemperate habits and violent temper" who had often whipped his wife, but there was "no positive proof, no eye witness." The paper's editorial added that he bore "a very bad character" and was said to have killed a man some time before.

Throughout August 15 a crowd of "colored people," men and women, gathered in and around the courthouse "vowing vengeance." They took up a collection, bought a rope, and kept it on display while declaring that they meant to hang the prisoner. The only peace officer seen that day was the constable, Louis Paoli, and no guard was posted at the jail.

About midnight the mob cut down the jail's gates and doors, took Stewart out, and hanged him; the coverage does not say where. His body was still hanging late on Tuesday. Wire briefs printed outside the state added that his father-in-law prayed for him and then helped to hang him, and one version described the lynchers as "a mob of colored men."

The Democrat-Star wrote that "the best citizens of the Bay" condemned the lynching and would act to have those responsible indicted, and its correspondent called on the next grand jury to repress such acts. No report of an inquest, arrest or indictment appears in the coverage. Three weeks later the Weekly Clarion of Jackson called the "recent Bay St. Louis wife murder" the second such case in the town, recalling an earlier one in which a Black man accused of murdering his white wife was freed from the jail by friends.

The fullest account ran in the Pascagoula Democrat-Star on August 19 under the headline "Mobbed for Murder," with a subhead calling the crime the "Supposed Murder of His Wife." In the same issue an editorial titled "Lynching at Bay St. Louis" called lynch law "a dangerous precedent," all the more so where the evidence was circumstantial, and warned that under mob law no innocent person would be safe. The correspondent placed the lynching beside other recent threats of mob action in the town and warned that next time a white man might be taken from jail "by a negro or a white mob."

Beyond the Gulf Coast the story traveled as one-sentence briefs that stated Stewart's guilt as fact. A version saying he "killed his wife with a hatchet" and that his father-in-law helped hang him ran between August 25 and September 2 in papers in Missouri, Wisconsin, Minnesota, South Carolina and West Virginia. The Washington Evening Star and the Cambria Freeman of Pennsylvania called the father-in-law's part "a peculiarity" of the lynching of "a Mississippi wife murderer," and the Washington Evening Critic turned it into a joke about fathers-in-law.

A second brief, reporting that "a negro wifemurderer was forcibly taken from jail by a mob of colored men and hanged," appeared from August 24 in papers in Arkansas, Kansas, Louisiana and Mississippi. In Mississippi, the American Citizen of Canton printed that version, while the Southern Herald of Liberty gave the date as the night of the 15th.

The wire briefs stated flatly that Stewart killed his wife with a hatchet, while the Democrat-Star, which reported on the hearing, found a "strong presumption" of guilt but no positive proof or eyewitness.

A mob, preceded by a crowd of men and women vowing vengeance, cut down the jail doors and hanged Stewart without trial for the alleged murder of his wife (A2, A4); the local paper called it 'lynching' and 'mob law' (A1, A2).
